title: AI Hiring in India Just Surged 16%. The Rest of the IT Industry Is Shrinking.
excerpt: A Naukri report shows AI roles grew 16% year-on-year in June while overall IT jobs fell 3% — the clearest sign yet that India's $315 billion tech sector is splitting into two economies.
body:
India's IT industry is splitting in two. On one side, companies are racing to hire AI specialists at a pace that has no precedent in recent memory. On the other, the broader technology workforce is contracting — and the gap between these two realities is widening every month.

Hiring for AI roles within India's IT sector surged 16% year-on-year in June, even as overall IT recruitment fell 3%, according to the latest JobSpeak report from Naukri, one of India's largest job portals. The data, drawn from listings across more than 150,000 firms, paints a picture of an industry undergoing a structural transformation at speed.

"The divergence is important because it shows where tech companies are still investing," said Hitesh Oberoi, CEO at Info Edge, which owns Naukri. "AI is increasingly becoming a core capability area, especially as demand shifts towards more senior and specialised talent."

## The TCS Signal

The numbers land in an industry already rattled by what its biggest player has said publicly. Tata Consultancy Services, India's largest software exporter, said last month that it expects IT companies to slow down hiring significantly. The firm's ambition is striking: TCS wants to eventually have an equal number of employees and AI agents in its workforce.

That is not a distant aspiration. TCS cut more than 12,000 jobs in the last fiscal year. Its total headcount fell by more than 23,000 on a net basis in the year ending March 2026. When the industry leader is actively reducing humans in favour of machines, the downstream effects ripple through every staffing model, every campus recruitment cycle, every H-1B petition.

## Across All Sectors, AI Is the Only Growth Story

The trend extends well beyond IT. Across 14 sectors tracked by Naukri, AI and machine learning job postings increased 25% year-on-year. Insurance and consumer goods companies showed the highest growth in overall hiring during the period, but within every sector, the AI-specific roles were the ones that grew fastest.

This creates a paradox that the diaspora knows intimately. Indian tech professionals are disproportionately represented in exactly the roles — software development, testing, project management, systems administration — that AI is automating. The people who built the outsourcing industry are now watching their own functions get compressed.

## What This Means for NRIs

For the estimated 300,000 Indian IT professionals working on H-1B visas in the United States, the bifurcation is not academic. Companies sponsoring their visas are the same ones restructuring their workforces around AI. An engineer whose role is classified as "IT services" rather than "AI development" faces a fundamentally different career trajectory than they did even two years ago.

The upside is real for those who make the transition. AI specialists with Indian engineering backgrounds are among the most sought-after professionals globally. The 16% hiring surge for AI roles in India reflects a domestic market that is still building capacity, and Indian professionals who can demonstrate AI competency carry that advantage into every immigration conversation.

But the transition is not painless, and it is not automatic. India's engineering colleges produce roughly 1.5 million graduates a year. If the IT industry is no longer absorbing them in bulk while simultaneously shedding experienced staff, the math changes for the entire pipeline — from campus to cubicle to consulate.

## The Bigger Picture

India's $315 billion IT industry has been under pressure from two directions simultaneously: clients holding back on spending due to macroeconomic uncertainty, and AI threatening the traditional business model of labour-intensive outsourcing.

The Naukri data suggests the industry is responding by concentrating investment in AI while allowing the broader workforce to shrink. Whether that makes India's tech sector more competitive or more fragile depends entirely on how fast the human capital can be retooled.

The 16% surge in AI hiring is a sign of life. The 3% decline in everything else is a sign of what comes next.
